clue.text: Mainly feeling poorly?

parts.note: surface reading: for the most part feeling unwell
setter's reading: on the main, the open ocean, and feeling ill because of it

explanation.surface: Someone describes their health as mostly under par.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mainly' looks like 'mostly', but the main is an old word for the sea, so this is sickness caused by being at sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Nausea brought on by a ship's motion is the condition of a sailor ill on the main.

clue.text: The French soldiers in alien water, for example

indicators.note: the word in means the preceding pieces sit inside the following word

parts.note: ET, the film's extraterrestrial
the French masculine definite article
ordinary soldiers are men

explanation.surface: French troops are stranded in some unfamiliar water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Alien water' reads as a phrase, but the definition starts at 'water'.
explanation.definitionFit: Water was one of the four classical elements, alongside earth, air and fire.

clue.text: Dance? What sauce!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a lively Latin American dance
second meaning: a spicy Mexican tomato relish

explanation.surface: Someone is outraged at the cheek of being asked to dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What sauce!' sounds like a protest at impudence; here sauce is a literal condiment.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spanish word names both a Latin dance style and a chunky spicy condiment served with tortilla chips.

clue.text: After tea, dare to play a parlour game

indicators.note: after says the next piece follows the first one in the answer

parts.note: cha is slang for tea

indicators.note: to play with letters is to move them about into a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written, to be shuffled

explanation.surface: After afternoon tea, the family dares each other into a party game.
explanation.walkthrough: CHA is old British slang for tea; it comes first because the rearranged dare goes after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A guessing game in which players mime words syllable by syllable is a classic Victorian drawing-room pastime.

clue.text: Heartlessly, your daughter hurries back to finish the cycle

indicators.note: going back means the whole string is read from right to left
without its heart, only the outside letters of the word survive

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word
D is the standard abbreviation for daughter
to nip is to go quickly

explanation.surface: A cruel parent's daughter rushes back to complete a bike ride.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cycle' suggests bicycles, but it is a washing machine's programme; the whole of YR, D and NIPS reverses together.
explanation.definitionFit: The final stage of a washing-machine programme spins clothes fast to fling water out, drying them.

clue.text: Photograph? I also have some bottles

indicators.note: the words have some of the answer, containing it within their run of letters

parts.note: found running across the end of the first word and into the next two

explanation.surface: Someone asks for a photo and adds that they also own some bottles.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark breaks the surface but not the letter string.
explanation.definitionFit: Small glass vessels for medicines or perfumes are little bottles.

clue.text: Person next door may be in rough trouble

indicators.note: in trouble, things are thrown into disorder, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: all nine letters of these three words

explanation.surface: A warning that the people next door might be having a hard time.
explanation.definitionFit: The one living beside you is the classic sense of the word.

clue.text: Study suitable way to make second change

parts.note: to read a subject is to study it at university
fitting or appropriate

explanation.surface: Advice that studying is the right way to adjust a second time.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage you 'read' a subject at university, meaning study it.
explanation.definitionFit: The prefix re- means again, so to adapt once more is to alter a second time.

clue.text: Giving someone his cards again is a con

definitions.meaning: first meaning, taken literally: handing out a second hand of cards

explanation.surface: Firing someone and then dismissing them a second time is a swindle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Giving someone his cards' is British for sacking them; the setter means dealing playing cards twice.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying one thing while doing another is treachery, a swindle; read literally, the phrase means dealing a second time.

clue.text: Timber trade

definitions.meaning: first meaning: pine or fir wood in planks
second meaning: to do business, buy and sell

explanation.surface: A two-word ad for the lumber business.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names softwood boards and also means to do business in goods.

clue.text: Lacking interest in government affairs, according to survey about it and CIA's involvement

parts.note: A as in French à, from à la, meaning in the manner of

indicators.note: about means wrapped around what follows

parts.note: an opinion poll surveys people

indicators.note: involvement suggests something tangled up, so these letters are mixed

parts.note: taken as written
the US intelligence agency, to be shuffled

explanation.surface: A poll suggests the public are bored by politics and spy agency meddling.
explanation.walkthrough: The survey's two L's split around the inner pieces; the leading A is a loose reading of 'according to', from French à as in à la.
explanation.definitionFit: The prefix a- means not, so someone not political has no interest in or commitment to party matters.

clue.text: Little Cameron came back in an awful state

indicators.note: in places the first piece inside the second
coming back means travelling the other way, so the name is read in reverse

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

indicators.note: something awful is in a mess, so the two letters swap around

parts.note: short form of David, as in the British prime minister David Cameron

explanation.surface: A political leader returns in a terrible condition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Awful state' reads as one condition, but 'state' alone is the US state; David Cameron led the British Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: A desert region in the western USA whose biggest city is Las Vegas is one of the fifty states.

clue.text: Wall retaining body and brain

parts.note: the main mass or body of something
the head houses the brain

explanation.surface: A wall that keeps in both body and brain, like a skull.
explanation.definitionFit: A partition dividing compartments in a ship or aircraft is an internal wall.

clue.text: Grooms plunge dagger into man holding me

parts.note: to thrust a knife in

indicators.note: holding something means having it inside, so the man's name surrounds the next word

parts.note: Len, a man's name
taken as written

explanation.surface: Bridegrooms knife a man who has seized the speaker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grooms' suggests bridegrooms, but here it is the noun for horse handlers.
explanation.definitionFit: Workers who look after horses in a stable are grooms, the plural noun.

clue.text: "Ladep" translated means to retract a previous opinion

parts.note: surface reading: a foreign word being rendered in English
setter's reading: the nonsense word is a cycling term written the wrong way round

explanation.surface: A dictionary entry for a made-up foreign word.
explanation.walkthrough: Ladep is no language; read it backwards, and the instruction 'back' plus the word you get forms the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Reversing the push on a bicycle's cranks is a figure for withdrawing from an earlier stance.

clue.text: Main supplier organising a new rota

indicators.note: organising puts things into a new order, so the letters are rearranged
a new version of something is reworked, backing up the call to rearrange

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: The chief provider is drawing up a fresh schedule.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Main supplier' sounds like a business; it is the body's main artery supplying blood.
explanation.definitionFit: The largest artery carries oxygenated blood from the heart to the whole body, so it is the chief supply line.

clue.text: City high flyers turnover is nonsense

indicators.note: to turn something over is to flip it, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: EC is the postcode district of the City of London
the Royal Air Force, whose pilots fly high

explanation.surface: The financial district's staff churn is absurd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'City high flyers turnover' reads like banking jargon; the City is London's financial district, postcode EC.
explanation.definitionFit: A ridiculous situation or empty sham is a farce, named after the comic stage genre.

clue.text: Posh car required in any divorce settlement

indicators.note: needed in means placed inside the following word

parts.note: taken as written
short for limousine, a luxury car

explanation.surface: Any divorce deal requires the luxury car to be handed over.
explanation.definitionFit: Maintenance money paid to a former spouse is a standard part of a divorce agreement.

clue.text: The speed with which Beckham originally is accepted as an A-lister

indicators.note: being accepted means being taken in, so this letter goes inside

parts.note: a formal word for swiftness

indicators.note: originally points to the very start of the name, its first letter

parts.note: the footballer's surname, first letter only

explanation.surface: How quickly David Beckham was welcomed into the top rank of fame.
explanation.walkthrough: CELERITY is a rare word for speed; the B goes after its fourth letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A top-tier famous person, on the A-list of invitations, is a star or celeb.

clue.text: Drug box to reveal grass

parts.note: E is slang for ecstasy
to box is to spar
taken as written

explanation.surface: A drugs raid opens a box and finds cannabis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grass' looks like the slang for cannabis, which fits 'drug'; here it is a real plant.
explanation.definitionFit: A tough Spanish and North African plant used for paper and rope is a kind of grass.

clue.text: Putting a label on the probation service's tool

definitions.meaning: first meaning: attaching a label or tag
second meaning: electronic monitoring of offenders

explanation.surface: A label for the probation office's gadget.
explanation.definitionFit: Fitting offenders with ankle devices that track them is electronic monitoring, the same word as labelling.

clue.text: Published for children on 1st December

parts.note: a person's offspring are their issue
the first letter of December

explanation.surface: A children's title came out at the start of December.
explanation.walkthrough: '1st December' reads as a date but means the month's first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A book or magazine that has been released to the public has been put out.

clue.text: Getting rid of the loss paid off

indicators.note: off means gone bad or out of order, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: all eight letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A business writes off a debt that has been settled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Paid off' reads as one phrase; 'off' is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Throwing something away or selling it off is its removal, a noun matching the gerund.

clue.text: Promise to provide hock

definitions.meaning: second meaning: to pawn something as security

explanation.surface: A vow to supply some German white wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hock' looks like the German wine; here it is slang for pawning.
explanation.definitionFit: A vow is a solemn undertaking, and to pawn an item is to deposit it as security for a loan.

clue.text: More than one soldier in the uprising

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising up means the letters read from bottom to top
in sets the soldier inside the following word

parts.note: taken as written
GI, an American soldier

explanation.surface: Several soldiers took part in the revolt.
explanation.walkthrough: The soldier sits inside the word the, and the whole lot is then read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Any number above one fits loosely; the setter picks a number bigger than one, a deliberately vague definition.

clue.text: Bird able to run the marathon?

definitions.text: Bird able to run the marathon?

parts.note: surface reading: a fast-running American cuckoo
setter's reading: an athlete who races on public streets

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a particular bird could manage a long-distance race.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful second reading of the bird's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A desert cuckoo of the American southwest famous for sprinting along roads, made famous by the cartoon.

clue.text: Get a drink outside

indicators.note: outside means the drink wraps around the letter

parts.note: a spirit
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is told to fetch a drink from outdoors.
explanation.definitionFit: To obtain or acquire something is to get it.

clue.text: They provide screens for viewers

parts.note: surface reading: television makers supplying sets to an audience
setter's reading: viewers are eyes, and the screens are the folds of skin that cover them

explanation.surface: A company supplies TV screens for its audience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Screens' suggests TVs; 'viewers' are eyes, which these shield.
explanation.definitionFit: The skin flaps that close over the eyes shield them, so they act as covers for the organs of sight.

clue.text: Does his return depend on how old the army is?

definitions.text: Does his return depend on how old the army is?

parts.note: a host is an old word for an army
your age is how old you are

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a captive's release hinges on the age of the troops holding him.
explanation.walkthrough: The army comes first in the answer although 'how old' comes first in the clue; a host is an archaic army, as in heavenly host.
explanation.definitionFit: A captive whose release is bargained for depends on the captors, here pictured as an army.
